title: The Inconvenient Figure
body: The utilisation rate for your division's flagship scheme came in at 31%. Your director asks, mildly, whether it might be "presented as a range rather than a number".

choices.text: Present it as a range.
choices.outcome: The slide reads "30-60%". Nobody asks. Your director says nothing further about it, which you decide to read as approval.

choices.text: Present the number.
choices.outcome: The meeting runs forty minutes over. The scheme is reviewed. You are not invited to the next one, or the four after that. It is noted.

choices.text: Present the number, with a recovery plan attached.
choices.outcome: You spend the weekend on eleven slides nobody asked for. The director presents them as his own. The scheme survives. So do you.

title: The Report
body: A consultancy has been engaged for $1.9 million to study the problem. Their final deck recommends, in different words, the thing you wrote in a minute paper two years ago.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let them have it.
choices.outcome: The recommendation is adopted enthusiastically. At the townhall it is described as "a fresh external perspective". You clap.

choices.text: Circulate your old minute paper.
choices.outcome: The email is received in silence by fourteen people. One of them, a deputy secretary you have never met, replies only to you: "Noted. Good paper." You keep that email for years. It is noted.

choices.text: Ask the consultants, in the Q&A, what their data source was.
choices.outcome: It was you. It was your minute paper. The room enjoys this more than the partner does.

title: Public Sector Transformation
body: Two days offsite. There are post-its. You have been asked to ideate on how the division might become "more agile, more citizen-centric, and more data-driven" without additional headcount or budget.

choices.text: Write down what everyone is actually thinking.
choices.outcome: Your post-it says "we need three more officers". The facilitator photographs the wall. Your post-it does not appear in the deck. It is noted.

choices.text: Produce an acronym.
choices.outcome: You offer S.E.R.V.E. The facilitator writes it in green marker. It appears on a banner in the lift lobby for the next six years.

choices.text: Volunteer to write the follow-up implementation plan.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted it. It becomes the only document from the offsite that anyone reads, which makes it, quietly, yours.

variants.title: Design Thinking
variants.body: A design-thinking sprint. There is a journey map on the wall, a persona called "Auntie Mary", and a facilitator who has asked everyone to put their assumptions in a box on the whiteboard marked PARKING LOT.

choices.text: Park the assumption everyone actually has.
choices.outcome: You write "no new resources" on a sticky note and put it in the parking lot. The facilitator laughs, then stops laughing, then moves it to a corner. It is noted.

choices.text: Give Auntie Mary a tagline.
choices.outcome: "Auntie Mary: Served Once, Served Right." It is printed on a tote bag. You see the tote bag at hawker centres for years.

choices.text: Volunteer to turn the wall into a plan.
choices.outcome: Nobody else wanted the wall. Your plan is the only thing from the sprint that survives the sprint, which makes it, quietly, yours.

variants.title: The Retreat
variants.body: A transformation retreat at a hotel on Sentosa. The breakout rooms are named after the organisation's values. You have been assigned to Integrity, which is the room with no window.

choices.text: Say, in Integrity, what the room is for.
choices.outcome: You say the division needs three more officers, not a fourth value. The room agrees in silence. The scribe does not write it down. It is noted.

choices.text: Coin a value.
choices.outcome: You propose "Ownership with Heart". It is adopted by the afternoon and on a lanyard by the end of the quarter.

choices.text: Volunteer to write up the retreat.
choices.outcome: You write it up properly, with owners and dates. It is the only retreat report anyone has ever acted on, and you are now, somehow, in charge of it.

title: A Word You Have Not Heard Before
body: Over lunch, a friend in HR mentions your CEP. You ask what that is. There is a pause of exactly the wrong length, and then a change of subject.

choices.text: Press her on it.
choices.outcome: Currently Estimated Potential. The highest grade the service thinks you will ever reach. It is decided about you, reviewed without you, and never disclosed to you. You think about this in the lift, and then most days after that.

choices.text: Let it go.
choices.outcome: You let it go. You will hear the term again, years from now, in a sentence that begins "well, realistically".

title: The Nomination
body: Two names from your division go forward for the Public Service Leadership Programme. Your director asks for your view on who should be put up.

choices.text: Nominate yourself.
choices.outcome: It is not done, saying it out loud. It is also not forbidden. You go. Your CEP is revised upward by a committee you will never meet.

choices.text: Nominate the obvious scholar.
choices.outcome: He was going anyway. He thanks you warmly and genuinely, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Nominate the quiet officer who does all the actual work.
choices.outcome: She is astonished. She goes. She rises faster than you do, and she never once forgets who put her name in.

title: The Thing That Actually Happens
body: It begins at 4am on a Saturday. By Monday there are three ministries, a task force, and a press conference scheduled for 6pm that somebody has to prepare a holding statement for.

choices.text: Take the pen. Write the statement.
choices.outcome: Eleven drafts. The Minister delivers the ninth almost verbatim. On Tuesday the Perm Sec asks for your name, and is told it, and writes it down.

choices.text: Run the operations room instead. Let someone else write.
choices.outcome: You are extremely good at this and nobody outside the room will ever know it happened. The thing does not get worse. That was the entire job.

choices.text: Stay out of it. It is not your division.
choices.outcome: It was not your division. That is true, and it is the sort of true thing that gets remembered in a particular tone.

title: The Forum Page
body: A member of the public has written to the Straits Times Forum about your scheme. The letter is 340 words, deeply aggrieved, and correct on every factual point.

choices.text: Draft a reply thanking him for his feedback.
choices.outcome: Your reply explains that the scheme is regularly reviewed. It is 310 words and says nothing. It is cleared in a single round, which tells you everything about what clears easily.

choices.text: Draft a reply that concedes his point and says what you will change.
choices.outcome: It goes through nine rounds of clearance and emerges shorter but intact. He writes again, to thank you. That one does not get published.

choices.text: Find out who he is.
choices.outcome: He is a retired schoolteacher in Ang Mo Kio. You look at his address on your screen for a while and then close the window, but you did open it.

title: The Posting
body: Three years in Washington, or Beijing, or Brussels. It is a good posting. Your daughter is nine and has just settled into a school she loves.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Three good years. You come back with a network, a much better sense of how small the country is, and a daughter who has stopped mentioning her old school.

choices.text: Turn it down.
choices.outcome: "Family reasons" is accepted immediately, warmly, and with complete understanding, and it is written down.

choices.text: Ask for it to be deferred two years.
choices.outcome: It is deferred. It is not re-offered. Nobody ever tells you that it will not be re-offered; you simply notice, eventually, that it has not been.

title: The Tender
body: The evaluation is finely balanced between two vendors. The stronger proposal is from a firm whose director left your ministry eighteen months ago and still calls you by your first name.

choices.text: Award it. The proposal genuinely is better.
choices.outcome: It genuinely is better. You document your reasoning with unusual care, which is itself a kind of confession.

choices.text: Recuse yourself from the evaluation.
choices.outcome: The panel proceeds without you and awards it to the same firm. Your recusal memo sits in the file, where, years later, it will be the only reason nobody asks you anything.

choices.text: Award it to the other vendor to be safe.
choices.outcome: The project runs eleven months late. You were not wrong to worry about perception; you were wrong to let it decide.

title: Meet-the-People Session
body: A friend from your old school volunteers at her MP's branch and asks if you could help at the Meet-the-People Session: Tuesday nights, writing appeal letters for residents whose cases have, in almost every instance, already been correctly decided. It is a party branch. You are a civil servant, and neutral. She says lots of people help in their own time.

choices.text: Go every Tuesday for a year, in your own time.
choices.outcome: Fifty-one Tuesdays, in your own T-shirt, never the branch one. You learn more about how policy actually lands than in all your years of writing it. The MP notices you, which is the part that will matter later.

choices.text: Go a few times, enough to be seen.
choices.outcome: Enough to be seen by the people who were looking. Not enough to change your mind about anything.

choices.text: Decline. You are a civil servant, and you would like to stay a neutral one.
choices.outcome: Your friend says she completely understands. The branch secretary, who was standing next to her, also understands, and remembers.

title: The Officer You Are Supervising
body: He is twenty-six, extremely clever, on the Administrative Service, and will outrank you in about four years. He has asked you to review his paper. It is not good.

choices.text: Tell him plainly, and teach him.
choices.outcome: He takes it well, rewrites it twice, and becomes rather good. He will outrank you soon, and he will remember.

choices.text: Clear it. Let him find out the hard way.
choices.outcome: He presents it. It goes badly. He is moved to a better posting three months later anyway, which teaches him a different lesson than the one you intended.

choices.text: Rewrite it yourself overnight.
choices.outcome: It is now a good paper with his name on it. He thanks you. He does not learn to write, and he does not need to.

title: The Leak
body: A policy under discussion has appeared, in accurate detail, on a Telegram channel. The circulation list was eleven people. You are one of them.

choices.text: Cooperate fully with the internal inquiry.
choices.outcome: It takes four months. It concludes that the source could not be determined. The eleven of you are never quite the same with each other again.

choices.text: Quietly work out who it was. Tell no one.
choices.outcome: It took you a fortnight. It was the one you would not have guessed, for a reason you find you have some sympathy with. You keep it.

choices.text: It was you.
choices.outcome: It was you, and you had what you still believe were good reasons. The inquiry does not find you. You wait years to find out whether that holds.

title: The Pingat
body: You are on the list for a National Day Award. It is the entry-level one. Your family will be extremely proud and will not understand which one it is.

choices.text: Accept, and bring your family to the investiture.
choices.outcome: Your family dresses as if for a wedding and photographs everything, including the carpet. It is, you realise afterwards, the best day they have had in years, and it cost you nothing.

choices.text: Accept, and ask that your team be recognised too.
choices.outcome: You are told the quota is fixed. You give the medal's mention at the division meeting entirely to them, which is not the same thing, and they know it is not, and it still lands.

title: Lo Hei
body: The divisional Chinese New Year lunch. The Permanent Secretary is at your table. There are eleven minutes of toss-and-auspicious-phrases and then a genuine, unhurried question directed at you: "So — what do you actually think we're getting wrong?"

choices.text: Tell her. Specifically. With an example.
choices.outcome: You have about ninety seconds and you use all of them. She listens without eating. At the end she says "say that again on Thursday, to the committee", and you realise you have just been promoted in every sense except the paperwork.

choices.text: Something safe about communications.
choices.outcome: "Mm," she says, and turns to the person on her left, and that is the whole of it.

choices.text: Deflect the question back to her.
choices.outcome: She answers it at length and very well. You learn a great deal. She learns nothing about you, which was the question.

title: The Inter-Ministry Committee
body: An IMC has been convened. It has met eleven times. Its interim finding is that further study is warranted. You are the secretariat.

choices.text: Write a paper that forces a decision.
choices.outcome: Your paper presents three options and recommends one. Two ministries object. A decision is made anyway, largely to stop the paper circulating. It is noted.

choices.text: Keep taking excellent minutes.
choices.outcome: Your minutes are widely admired. The committee meets fourteen more times. You are commended for your support of the committee's work.

choices.text: Leak the deadlock to a friendly journalist.
choices.outcome: A decision follows within a month. You had been right about what needed to happen and wrong about how, and only one of those is survivable.

title: The Ballot
body: Fourth BTO application. Non-mature estate, four-room. At work you are, technically, the government.

choices.text: Ballot again like everyone else.
choices.outcome: Queue number 2,847 of 610 units. You laugh in the lift. At the next family dinner you are noticeably better at explaining the scheme, because now you have also lost.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB whether anything is coming up.
choices.outcome: There is nothing improper in what he tells you — it is all public, three weeks early. That is the whole of the impropriety, and you both know its exact size.

choices.text: Buy resale. Take the loan.
choices.outcome: Done by Thursday. The cash-over-valuation hurts for eleven years, and you never again have to explain a queue number at a family dinner.

variants.title: The Prime Launch
variants.body: This launch is a Prime project: a central location, a lower price now, a clawback of the subsidy when you sell, and a minimum occupation period of ten years. The queue is already longer than the estate.

choices.text: Apply, and take your chances.
choices.outcome: Queue number 1,206 for 290 units. You do the arithmetic once, and then decide not to do it again.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB how the next launch looks.
choices.outcome: He tells you which launch next quarter will have the shorter queue. It is on the website three weeks later, word for word. For three weeks, you were the website.

choices.text: Buy resale instead, and stop thinking about it.
choices.outcome: You buy a 1990s five-room with its original kitchen cabinets and a view of a multi-storey carpark. The loan is long. The cabinets are, it turns out, very good.

variants.title: The Fifth Ballot
variants.body: Fifth application. The ballot results page now remembers you. Your queue numbers, laid end to end, would house a small town.

choices.text: Ballot again.
choices.outcome: Queue number 3,104. You screenshot it for a group chat that has become, over five years, mainly a support group.

choices.text: Ask a friend at HDB what is coming up.
choices.outcome: He walks you through next quarter's launches over kopi. Every word of it goes on the website three weeks later. You have, technically, only had your kopi early.

choices.text: Buy resale. Take the loan.
choices.outcome: Done in a week. The valuation comes in below the price, and the difference has to be paid in cash, which is the rule and is also most of your savings.

title: Committee of Supply
body: The COS cuts. Your Minister has eight minutes and needs one announceable thing. Your division has nothing ready, and nobody in the room wants to be the one who says so.

choices.text: Announce the pilot you have been quietly building.
choices.outcome: It is eighteen months from ready. It is announced as though it is four. You spend the next eighteen months making the announcement retroactively true, and you manage it, mostly.

choices.text: Rebrand an existing scheme with a new name and a higher number.
choices.outcome: "Enhanced". It is enhanced by the word "enhanced". It is covered favourably. Nobody is harmed and nothing is gained and this is, you suspect, most of what happens here.

choices.text: Tell the Minister there is nothing, and say so early.
choices.outcome: He is annoyed for a day and grateful for a year, because the alternative was being annoyed in Parliament. He does not forget either part. It is noted.

title: The Reorganisation
body: Your division is being moved to another ministry. The rationale runs to forty slides. Nobody in your division was consulted, and the new org chart has one fewer director-level box than the old one.

choices.text: Fight for your people's postings first.
choices.outcome: You place all nine of them before you place yourself. You end up in the worst of the remaining boxes. They know exactly what you did and one of them will be in a position to repay it.

choices.text: Secure the good box for yourself first.
choices.outcome: You get it. It is a good box. The nine of them are placed adequately, and something in the division's manner toward you changes in a way that is never once spoken aloud.

choices.text: Volunteer to run the transition.
choices.outcome: Nine months of thankless plumbing. It goes unusually smoothly, which means nobody notices, except the two people whose opinion of you decides your next five years.

title: The Engagement Exercise
body: A national conversation. Eleven hundred citizens across forty sessions. You are writing the synthesis report. The feedback is overwhelmingly about cost of living and it does not fit the three pillars the report was designed around.

choices.text: Add a fourth pillar.
choices.outcome: The design is spoiled and the report is true. It is published with the fourth pillar looking slightly bolted on, because it was, because it had to be.

choices.text: Distribute the feedback across the three existing pillars.
choices.outcome: It fits beautifully. The launch is well received. Somewhere in a file there is a spreadsheet of what eleven hundred people actually said, and it is not the report.

choices.text: Publish the raw feedback alongside the report.
choices.outcome: This has not been done before. It is permitted, eventually, after a fortnight of anxiety at three levels. It is the single most-read government document of the year. It is noted.

title: The New Reporting Officer
body: Your reporting officer has moved on. The new one arrives from a different ministry, knows nothing about you, and has brought two people she trusts from her old division.

choices.text: Make yourself indispensable on the hardest file.
choices.outcome: It takes eight months and it works. She is a better RO than the last one and rates you honestly, which is the first time that has happened.

choices.text: Be useful to her two people.
choices.outcome: You become the one who knows where things are. It is a real position and a small one, and you hold it for four years.

choices.text: Keep your head down until she leaves.
choices.outcome: She stays five years. Your appraisals during that period are a flat line that will be visible to every promotion board for the rest of your career.

title: The Secondment
body: A two-year secondment to a statutory board that is, everyone agrees, in some difficulty. It is not a promotion. It is either a proving ground or a siding, and nobody will tell you which.

choices.text: Go, and fix it.
choices.outcome: It was a proving ground. You find out which it was only by how the phone starts ringing in month twenty-two.

choices.text: Go, and keep your head down for two years.
choices.outcome: It becomes a siding. Sidings are not assigned; they are accepted.

choices.text: Refuse it and stay where you are visible.
choices.outcome: You stay visible doing work of no consequence, which turns out to be a worse place to be seen than a hard job nobody watched.

title: The Adviser Suggests Something
body: After a community event, the constituency's grassroots adviser mentions — apparently in passing, definitely not in passing — that you handle yourself well with people.

choices.text: Say you have thought about it.
choices.outcome: You have not said yes to anything. You have said the one thing that gets your name written on a different list.

choices.text: Laugh it off.
choices.outcome: He laughs too, and the subject closes, and it is not reopened by him or by anyone for a very long time.

title: The Figure, Again
body: An audit of the scheme has requested the original utilisation data for the year you presented as a range. The request is routine. It is addressed to you by name.

choices.text: Provide everything. Explain the presentation decision.
choices.outcome: You write it down plainly, including the part where you were asked. It is accepted with a coolness that lasts about two years and then, oddly, becomes a kind of respect.

choices.text: Provide the range, and say the raw file was not retained.
choices.outcome: The file was retained. It is retained in three places. You have now told an auditor something untrue in writing, which is a different category of thing from what you did years ago.

title: Questions About the Tender
body: A parliamentary question has been filed about procurement from firms with former public-sector directors. Your award is one of fourteen in the annex.

choices.text: Your documentation was meticulous. Let it speak.
choices.outcome: It is meticulous. The PQ is answered in eleven lines and the annex is never discussed. The care you took at the time was the entire defence, and you took it because you knew you would need it.

choices.text: Ask a friend to keep your award out of the annex.
choices.outcome: It stays out. Two people now know why it stayed out, and one of them is not you.

title: A Journalist Has Been Asking
body: Someone is reconstructing an old story and has been calling people who were on a circulation list years ago. They have now called you.

choices.text: Decline to comment. Say nothing to anyone.
choices.outcome: The story runs without you in it, this time. You spend a fortnight discovering exactly how much of your composure was borrowed against never being asked.

choices.text: Go to the most senior person you answer to, and tell them everything first, yourself.
choices.outcome: It is the worst forty minutes of your career and it ends the matter permanently. You are thanked for coming forward. It is meant, and it is also never forgotten.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Deputy Secretary now. She has been asked for names for a post that is, everyone understands, the last rung before the very top.

choices.text: Let her decide without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She puts your name in. She does not mention the nomination from years ago and neither do you, because the whole point of the thing was that it was not a transaction, and it stays one by not being named.

choices.text: Tell her, before she decides, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She puts your name in anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Deputy Secretary now, several rungs above you, and she has a post to fill in her division. She asks for you by name.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: She does not mention the nomination from years ago and neither do you. She simply gives you the hardest file in the division and reads your work twice.

choices.text: Tell her, first, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She asks for you anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Permanent Secretary now, younger than you and faster. She has been asked for names for a Permanent Secretary post, which everyone understands is the last rung there is.

choices.text: Let her decide without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She puts your name in. She does not mention the nomination from years ago and neither do you, because the whole point of the thing was that it was not a transaction.

choices.text: Tell her, before she decides, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She puts your name in anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Permanent Secretary now too, and the two of you sit on the same committees. She has been asked, quietly, which of her colleagues might one day be invited to tea.

choices.text: Let her answer without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She gives one name. You find out which only by the way certain people start greeting you in lifts.

choices.text: Tell her, before she answers, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She gives your name anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Nominated
body: She is a Permanent Secretary now. The Prime Minister's office asks Permanent Secretaries, from time to time, for a frank view of the political office holders and Members they work with. She has been asked about you.

choices.text: Let her give it without hearing from you.
choices.outcome: She gives it. You never see it. At the next reshuffle, the commentary describes you as someone the civil service rates, which is the one review a politician never gets to read.

choices.text: Tell her, before she is asked, that she owes you nothing.
choices.outcome: She says she knows. She gives her view anyway, which is how you learn the difference between a debt and a judgement.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: He is your Deputy Secretary now. At the end of a routine meeting he stays behind and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he has put your name forward for something and that he did it on the strength of one afternoon, years ago. You go back to your desk and sit there for a while.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. He says it is the only performance review he has ever kept.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: He is a Deputy Secretary too now, on your corridor, at an age you will not ask about. At the end of a joint meeting he stays behind and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he has put your name forward for something, on the strength of one afternoon, years ago. You go back to your office and sit there for a while.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. He says it is the only performance review he has ever kept.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: He is one of your Deputy Secretaries now. At the end of a routine meeting he stays behind and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he tells his own officers the same things now, in the same words, and that they dislike it as much as he did. He says it as though this were the point. It was.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, for the first time in your presence, and agrees. He says it is the only performance review he has ever kept.

title: The Officer You Taught
body: He is a Permanent Secretary now. After he briefs a group of Members on a bill, he waits until the room is empty and says, without preamble, "You were the only person who ever told me my work was bad."

choices.text: Tell him he was worth the trouble.
choices.outcome: He says he will return the favour, and tell you when your speeches are bad. He does. They get better, and the newspapers notice before the party does.

choices.text: Tell him his paper was still bad.
choices.outcome: He laughs, and says that is why he writes your briefs himself now. They are very good. They are also eleven pages long, and he would like you to read all of them.

title: An Invitation to Tea
body: The email is from someone whose title is not explained. The venue is a room in a building you have walked past a thousand times. There is no agenda. Everyone in the country knows what this is.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: Tea is served. The conversation is about nothing for forty minutes. Then a second man arrives with a folder, and opens it, and reads.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You write three sentences and delete two of them. The reply thanks you for your candour. You are not asked again, and you will think about this for the rest of your life.

variants.body: A phone call, not an email. The voice is warm and unhurried and does not give a surname. Would you be free for lunch on Thursday? Nobody has ever been free for lunch on a Thursday the way you are suddenly free for lunch on this one.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: Lunch is at a club with carpet so thick it swallows footsteps. The conversation is about nothing for an hour. Then the coffee comes, and so does a second man, with a folder, and he opens it, and reads.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You say you are honoured, and committed to the service. The voice says it understands completely. It is the most understanding voice you will ever hear, and you never hear it again.

variants.body: A note on your desk, in a hand-delivered envelope, asking whether you might spare an hour for a conversation "about the future". It does not say whose.

choices.text: Go.
choices.outcome: The hour is in a quiet room with very good chairs. Two people ask for your views on the country, and then, without changing tone, open a folder and begin to read from it.

choices.text: Decline, politely.
choices.outcome: You reply by hand, because it seems right, and you say no. You are thanked, by hand, within a day. Then the future happens without you in it.

title: The Background Check
body: The same man, the same folder, a smaller room. He has read it all. He would like to hear it from you, and he is very good at not saying which parts he means.

choices.text: Disclose everything, including the things they may not have.
choices.outcome: He listens without writing anything until you have finished, and then writes for a long time.

choices.text: Answer exactly what is asked and nothing more.
choices.outcome: The questions are precise and you answer them precisely. He thanks you. Nobody mentions the folder again, which is how you know it is still there.

variants.body: A different room this time, with a window that does not open. Two people now: one asks, one writes. The folder is on the table between them, closed, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Tell them everything, including what is not in the folder.
choices.outcome: You talk for forty minutes. The one who writes fills four pages. The one who asks says, at the end, "Thank you. That was very complete," and it sounds like the highest praise either of them is allowed to give.

choices.text: Answer the questions you are asked, and only those.
choices.outcome: Precise questions, precise answers. Nobody opens the folder. When you leave it is still on the table, closed, and you understand that it will be opened later, somewhere else.

variants.body: The background check arrives first as a form: forty-two questions, three of them about companies you have never heard of and one about a company you have. Then a meeting, to "go through it together".

choices.text: Go through all of it, including question thirty-one.
choices.outcome: You go through everything, and then the things the form did not ask. The meeting runs an hour over. Nobody seems to mind; that appears to have been the point.

choices.text: Go through what is on the form.
choices.outcome: The form is answered completely and exactly. Question thirty-one is answered in eleven words. The meeting ends on time, and the folder goes back into a drawer you do not get to see.

title: The General Election
body: You are introduced at a press conference alongside four others. Nomination Day, then nine days of walkabouts in weather that is relentlessly, unhelpfully hot.

choices.text: Run in the GRC. Ride the team.
choices.outcome: Your name is fourth on a poster. You shake eleven thousand hands and understand, with total clarity, that almost none of this is about you.

choices.text: Ask for the single seat.
choices.outcome: A contested SMC, alone, against a decent opponent with a real ground game. Nobody carries you and nobody can blame anybody else.

variants.body: Polling Day is announced on a Monday. By Wednesday your face is on a lamp post outside a coffee shop you have never been into, and the coffee shop has opinions about your face.

choices.text: Stand in the GRC, with the team.
choices.outcome: You spend nine days learning which blocks have lifts that stop on every floor. The anchor minister does the rally speeches. You do the lifts.

choices.text: Ask for the single-member seat.
choices.outcome: A single seat, a real opponent, and nobody to share the swing with. Yours is the only name on your posters, which is thrilling for exactly one day.

variants.body: Nomination Day, in a school hall that smells of floor polish. Your papers are checked twice. Across the hall, an opposition candidate you once sat beside at a seminar waves, cheerfully, as if this were not happening.

choices.text: Stand with the team in the GRC.
choices.outcome: Nine days of walkabouts in a team of five. At every coffee shop someone asks which one you are. By the end, you can answer.

choices.text: Ask for the single seat.
choices.outcome: Nine days of being the only person anyone in the ward asks. By the last rally your voice has gone and your opponent's has not, which feels significant and is not.

title: The Maiden Speech
body: Convention grants it a courteous hearing and no interruptions. You have twelve minutes and the House is two-thirds empty.

choices.text: The safe speech about your constituency.
choices.outcome: Warm, local, unobjectionable, forgotten by dinner. Three colleagues tell you it was lovely.

choices.text: The one thing from your years in the service that you actually believe.
choices.outcome: It is quoted. Two of the quotations are the ones you meant and one is not. A Minister you have never met sends a one-line note: "That needed saying." It is noted.

title: The Town Council
body: A lift upgrading contract in your ward. The sinking fund does not cover it. The residents' committee has views, the contractor has a cousin, and you have signing authority.

choices.text: Do it properly and slowly. Explain the delay.
choices.outcome: Eight months of complaints at every MPS. The lifts are done correctly and under budget and nobody thanks you, and in four years the accounts are clean when somebody looks.

choices.text: Do it fast. Sort the paperwork after.
choices.outcome: The lifts are done in eleven weeks and the ward is delighted. The paperwork is sorted out approximately, which is a word that does not appear in the Town Councils Act.

title: The National Bonus
body: Your National Bonus is computed from four indicators, equally weighted: unemployment, real median income growth, real income growth at the 20th percentile, and real GDP growth. Each has a published target band (GDP growth of 2 to 4 per cent, for instance), and the formula is in the public domain. You now hold a portfolio that moves at least two of them.

choices.text: Push the policy that lifts incomes at the 20th percentile.
choices.outcome: It is expensive, unglamorous and works slowly. It also happens to be one of the four indicators in your own bonus formula. Both of these things are true and the second one is never mentioned by anybody, ever.

choices.text: Push headline GDP.
choices.outcome: Cleaner, faster, and it moves the one indicator everyone is watching. The bonus is six months, the maximum. You do not look closely at the distributional annex.

choices.text: Ask, in Cabinet, whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set.
choices.outcome: The question is received with great seriousness and complete stillness. It is minuted. It is answered thoroughly and it is not answered at all, and you have marked yourself out as a particular kind of colleague. It is noted.

title: The Correction Direction
body: A post about your ministry's scheme is circulating. It is misleading in two places and, awkwardly, correct in the third.

choices.text: Issue the correction direction.
choices.outcome: The correction notice appears. It is factually unimpeachable and addresses two of the three points. The third point continues to circulate, now with a grievance attached to it.

choices.text: Answer the third point publicly instead.
choices.outcome: You concede it in a Facebook post at 11pm written in your own words. It is shared more than anything your ministry has ever published, and half of the shares are from people who dislike you. It is noted.

title: The Reshuffle
body: The Prime Minister's office has asked to see you on Thursday. Nobody knows what about, and eleven people have told you they are sure it is good news.

choices.text: Ask for the hard ministry nobody wants.
choices.outcome: Housing, or health, or transport. Something with a queue and a waiting list and a headline every week. You are given it immediately, and the speed of the agreement tells you what it was going to be anyway.

choices.text: Ask to stay where you are.
choices.outcome: You stay. It is pleasant and important and nobody will ever find out whether you were any good, including you.

title: The Succession
body: The next generation of leadership is settling on a first among equals. The process is informal, which means it is entirely decided by people in a room, and you are in the room.

choices.text: Put yourself forward.
choices.outcome: You say it plainly, which is not the convention. The room absorbs it. Nothing is decided that day; but your name is now one of the two being weighed, instead of one of the nine being listed.

choices.text: Back the other candidate. Ask for a senior portfolio.
choices.outcome: He wins, obviously, and he knows exactly who delivered it. You get everything you asked for, and you will spend the rest of your career as the most powerful person in the room who is not him, which is not the thing you wanted.

title: The Work
body: A scheme goes out on time because you and four other people made it. It will never have your name on it. Nobody's name is on it; that is how you know it is real.

choices.text: Do the work well.
choices.outcome: It goes out on time. Nobody mentions it, which is what "on time" earns you.

choices.text: Do the work, and be seen doing it.
choices.outcome: You present it at the divisional meeting with four slides more than it needed. Two people now know your name who did not.

choices.text: Coast. You have earned a quiet year.
choices.outcome: You leave at six every day for a year, eat dinner at a normal hour, and it costs you exactly what you thought it would.

0: A scheme goes out on time. Five people know why. You are one of them.
You clear forty-one papers and write one sentence you are proud of. Nobody notices the sentence, which is how you know it was right.
A minute you wrote is quoted back to you, months later, as the ministry's position. You do not correct anyone.
1: You present the scheme at three different forums. By the third, you are the scheme.
Your name is on the slide, the email and the photograph. The work was mostly the same as last year's, which nobody mentions.
Someone from another ministry greets you by name in the lift. You have been seen, and the lift is evidence.
2: You do what is asked, on time, and not a minute more. Nobody complains, because nobody can find anything to complain about.
A quiet year at your desk. Your out-of-office message is the best thing you write.
The papers come in and go out. Somewhere on your floor someone is working late, and it is not you.

variants.body: A form that citizens fill in has eleven fields. Seven of them ask for things the government already knows. Removing them takes four agencies, two legal opinions and a year of meetings that will never be minuted as important.

choices.text: Do the work properly.
choices.outcome: Three fields go. The other four turn out to be required by a regulation nobody can find the reason for. Three is a good year.

choices.text: Do the work, and make sure the right people see it.
choices.outcome: Your one-page note on the three fields is circulated as "a good example of citizen-centric design". You will be asked to give the talk.

choices.text: Let the agencies sort it out among themselves.
choices.outcome: They do not. The form keeps its eleven fields. You keep your evenings, which you decide were also a public good.

variants.body: This year's work is a review of a review: what was recommended three years ago, what was done, and why the difference is described as "phased implementation".

choices.text: Write it straight.
choices.outcome: Your review says what happened. It is accepted with thanks, and its recommendations are, in due course, phased.

choices.text: Write it straight, and present it yourself.
choices.outcome: You show the gap between recommendation and implementation in a chart so clear that two directors ask for the slide. One of them later uses it against you, admiringly.

choices.text: Write it the way the last one was written.
choices.outcome: It reads beautifully and says nothing anyone could disagree with. It takes a week. You spend the rest of the year on other things, mostly lunch.

variants.body: A hotline takes two thousand calls a week. Four hundred are the same question, which the website answers on page six. Someone has to decide whether the problem is the callers or page six.

choices.text: Fix page six.
choices.outcome: Page six becomes page one, in plain words. Calls drop by a third. The hotline team sends a cake with no message, which is the highest honour a hotline can give.

choices.text: Fix page six, and present the call figures.
choices.outcome: Your before-and-after chart travels further than the website did. Two other agencies cite it in their own papers, with your name in the footnote.

choices.text: Note it for whoever owns the website, and go home on time.
choices.outcome: Your note is clear and lands in the right inbox, where it stays. The calls continue. You are home by half past six, most days.

variants.body: A circular has to reach forty agencies by the first of the month. It is on its ninth draft, and the ninth is the first one anyone outside this building could understand.

choices.text: Send the ninth draft, on time.
choices.outcome: It goes out on the twenty-eighth. Three agencies reply that it is the clearest circular they have had this year, which in agency terms is a standing ovation.

choices.text: Send it, and brief the agencies yourself.
choices.outcome: Forty agencies, four briefings, one set of slides. By the last one you can do it without the slides, and two directors now ask for you by name.

choices.text: Leave the last draft to the next person in the chain.
choices.outcome: It goes out on the third of the month. Nobody asks why it was late, and you were home for dinner on all three days.

title: The Appraisal Conversation
body: Forty minutes, a form with six competency domains, and a reporting officer who says "I'd like you to be more visible" without specifying to whom.

choices.text: Ask directly what your ceiling is.
choices.outcome: "That's not really something we discuss." The sentence is delivered kindly and it is a complete answer.

choices.text: Agree to be more visible.
choices.outcome: You volunteer for two committees. It works, in the sense that more people have now seen you.

choices.text: Ask what she needs that isn't being done.
choices.outcome: She thinks for a moment and then tells you something real. You do it. That conversation is worth the other thirty-nine minutes.

0: You ask about your ceiling again. Your reporting officer says it is "not a helpful way to think about it", which is the most precise answer you have had.
Forty minutes, six competency domains, and one question from you that nobody writes down.
1: You agree to be more visible. Your reporting officer agrees that you have been. Visibility is mentioned twice.
Six competency domains, one new acronym, and the phrase "stretch assignment". You nod at the right moments.
2: You ask what is not being done. There is a list. By March most of it is done, and you are on a new list.
Your reporting officer says the ranking exercise was "very tight this year". You ask what would have loosened it, and are told.

variants.body: The appraisal form has been redesigned. It now has four competency domains instead of six, a section called "Aspirations", and a box for your reporting officer's overall impression that is larger than all the others put together.

choices.text: Ask what the overall impression says.
choices.outcome: "It's still being calibrated." The form is turned face down, gently, the way people close the door on a sleeping room.

choices.text: Fill in "Aspirations" with something ambitious.
choices.outcome: You write "to lead a cross-agency effort". Within the month you are put on one, as a member. It is a start, and it is minuted as one.

choices.text: Ask which of the four domains actually counts.
choices.outcome: A pause, and then an honest answer: "Ownership." You spend the year owning things. It shows.

variants.body: Your appraisal is done over a video call, because your reporting officer is overseas. Her camera is off. Her connection is excellent. The forty minutes feel like ninety.

choices.text: Ask, plainly, where you stand.
choices.outcome: "You're doing fine." There is a long silence on the line, and then: "Fine is good." It is clearly not the whole sentence.

choices.text: Turn your camera on, and keep it on.
choices.outcome: Hers comes on too, eventually. The second half of the conversation is noticeably warmer. You are now, in a small way, visible.

choices.text: Ask what she would want done while she is away.
choices.outcome: She lists three things. You do two of them before she lands. She mentions it at the ranking meeting, which is the only meeting that matters.

variants.body: The appraisal is in a meeting room booked for thirty minutes. Your reporting officer arrives twelve minutes late, from another appraisal, carrying its form by mistake.

choices.text: Ask, while there is time, where your ceiling is.
choices.outcome: She looks at the form in her hand, which is not yours, and says that is above her pay grade. It may be the only literal thing said to you all year.

choices.text: Use the eighteen minutes to list what you did.
choices.outcome: You get through the list in eleven minutes. She writes down four items, and they are the four that end up in your ranking. You learn which four to lead with.

choices.text: Ask what she needs from you this year.
choices.outcome: She answers before she has sat down: a paper nobody has started. You start it that afternoon, and your next appraisal begins on time.

variants.body: This year's appraisal includes 360-degree feedback. One anonymous comment says you "never say no to anything from upstairs". It is meant, you think, as a complaint.

choices.text: Ask what the comment means for your ceiling.
choices.outcome: She says it is "a development point, not a ceiling point", and then that ceilings are not discussed. Both halves are true, and only one of them was an answer.

choices.text: Say you will be more visible, sideways as well as up.
choices.outcome: You start a monthly lunch for the people around you. Attendance is excellent. Next year's comment is about the lunches, and it is fond.

choices.text: Ask what she needs you to say no to.
choices.outcome: She names two things, immediately. You drop them both, and everyone around you notices before she does.

title: 11:40pm, Level 9
body: The clearance has come back with comments for the fourth time. The dinner you promised to be home for was at eight.

choices.text: Finish it tonight.
choices.outcome: Cleared at 1:20am. You are thanked in a one-word email. Dinner is in the fridge, with a note that is mostly punctuation.

choices.text: Go. Send it in the morning.
choices.outcome: You make it home for dessert. It goes in at 8:40am and the world does not end, and you note carefully that the world did not end.

0: Level 9 at 11pm becomes a habit, then a reputation.
The cleaner on your floor now says goodnight to you by name.
You miss a birthday dinner and make a deadline. Both are forgotten by March, by different people.
1: You leave at seven and send things in the morning. The things arrive. The building does not fall down.
A birthday dinner, attended. The comments on the fourth draft wait until morning, as comments always could.
You have stopped apologising for leaving on time. Two people on your floor have started doing the same.

variants.title: Sunday, 4pm
variants.body: Your niece's birthday party. An email from upstairs wants a brief by eight tomorrow morning, and everyone else at the table is holding cake.

choices.text: Find a quiet corner and write it now.
choices.outcome: You write it on your phone behind the cake table. It is cleared by nine. In the party photographs you are the back of a head, bent over a screen.

choices.text: Stay at the party. Write it at six tomorrow.
choices.outcome: You sing, badly, and cut the cake. The brief goes in at 7:55am. Upstairs never asks when it was written, which teaches you something you try to remember.

variants.title: 10:50pm, One Comment
variants.body: Your paper comes back with a single comment, sent at 10:50pm: "Can we tighten?" The paper is already two pages.

choices.text: Tighten it tonight.
choices.outcome: Two pages become one and a half. The half you cut was the only part anyone would have disagreed with, so the paper sails through.

choices.text: Reply that it is tight, and go to bed.
choices.outcome: You reply at 10:52pm that it is already tight, and go to bed. In the morning there is a thumbs-up, which in this building is a concession.

title: The Budget Round
body: Your bid is for eleven officers and a system. Finance has indicated that the envelope is flat.

choices.text: Bid big and justify every line.
choices.outcome: You get four officers and half a system, which is what you expected, having bid for eleven precisely so that four would look like a compromise.

choices.text: Bid exactly what you need.
choices.outcome: You get seventy percent of exactly what you needed, because the process assumes padding and punishes its absence.

choices.text: Don't bid. Absorb it.
choices.outcome: Finance is delighted. Your officers do the work of eleven people for three years and two of them leave.

0: You bid for eleven and get four, which is what you bid eleven for.
Budget season. Every line is justified, footnoted and cut by a third, as planned.
1: You bid for exactly what you need and get two-thirds of it, which Finance describes as a good outcome for you.
The envelope is flat. Your bid is honest. The two facts meet in a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet wins.
2: You absorb it again. Finance sends a note of thanks, which is the only budget increase you get.
Budget season. You learn a new way to say "absorb".

title: Tuesday Night
body: Meet-the-People Session. Forty-one residents, a queue to the lift lobby, and a man who has come every week for two years about a case that cannot be reopened.

choices.text: See every last one of them.
choices.outcome: You finish at 12:40am. You fix two things that were genuinely fixable. The man comes back next Tuesday, as he will for another nine years.

choices.text: Write the appeal letters properly.
choices.outcome: Eleven letters, each one actually argued rather than templated. Three succeed. Templated, none would have.

choices.text: Let the volunteers handle the tail.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten. The volunteers are entirely capable. Word still gets round that you left at ten.

0: Tuesday nights, every last case. The man whose case cannot be reopened brings you kueh.
Meet-the-People runs past midnight. The volunteers have started bringing their own chairs.
1: Forty letters a Tuesday, each one actually argued. Three a month succeed that would not have.
A resident's appeal, properly written, comes back approved. The resident thanks the volunteer who typed it, which is fair.
2: The volunteers handle the tail. They are very good at it, and they are getting tired.
A resident thanks you for something the Town Council did. You accept on its behalf, and leave at ten.

variants.title: Meet-the-People, After the Rain
variants.body: A downpour at seven, so everyone comes at nine. The queue includes a family whose flat appeal has been turned down twice, and a man who would like the void deck named after his father.

choices.text: Stay until the last one is seen.
choices.outcome: Past one in the morning. The void deck will not be renamed, and you tell him so kindly enough that he shakes your hand twice.

choices.text: Take the family's appeal, and write it yourself.
choices.outcome: Two pages, citing the right paragraph. The appeal succeeds on the third try, which the family credits to persistence and you credit to the paragraph.

choices.text: Leave the volunteers to finish.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten. The volunteers stay until one. By Thursday a resident has posted about the evening, and the post is about you leaving at ten.

variants.title: Tuesday Night, the Lift
variants.body: Thirty residents and one theme: a lift that has been under upgrading for eleven months. Nobody is angry with you. Everybody would like you to be angry on their behalf.

choices.text: See every one of them, one by one.
choices.outcome: Thirty conversations about the same lift. They all go home feeling heard, which is not the same as a lift but is not nothing.

choices.text: Write about the lift properly, tonight.
choices.outcome: Your letter names the contractor, the start date and the eleven months. A new completion date arrives within the week and is, for once, met.

choices.text: Let the volunteers take the rest.
choices.outcome: You leave at ten. Twenty-nine residents are seen about the lift. The thirtieth wanted you, and mentions it at every block party for a year.

title: The Walkabout
body: Wet market, 7:20am, a camera crew, and a stallholder who has strong and specific views about the price of chillies and is delighted to share them at volume.

choices.text: Listen to her properly, on camera.
choices.outcome: Four minutes of her talking and you not interrupting. It is clipped and shared widely, and the comments are, unusually, kind.

choices.text: Keep moving. Stay on schedule.
choices.outcome: Nineteen stalls in forty minutes. The photographs are excellent and no one remembers a word.

0: Wet markets, 7am, cameras. You now know the price of chillies better than the price of anything else.
An auntie tells you that you looked thinner on television. You listen to the rest of what she says, which is about the lift.
1: A walkabout in the rain, on schedule. The photograph of you holding someone else's umbrella does very well.
Eleven stalls in forty minutes. Everyone gets a handshake and nobody gets a sentence.

variants.title: The Hawker Centre
variants.body: Lunchtime at a hawker centre, with photographers. The uncle at the drinks stall would like to explain, in detail, why his rent has gone up and what he thinks should be done about it.

choices.text: Sit down and hear him out.
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes, one kopi going cold, and you follow up on his rent in writing. The one photographer who stayed gets the best picture of the day.

choices.text: Buy a kopi, smile, and keep moving.
choices.outcome: You pay for the kopi, smile for the photograph and move on. In the photograph, he is still talking.

variants.title: The Estate Visit
variants.body: Eight blocks before lunch and a ribbon to cut. A resident on a mobility scooter would like to show you a ramp that does not quite reach the kerb.

choices.text: Go and look at the ramp.
choices.outcome: You walk the ramp with her, slowly, cameras behind you. It is two centimetres short. It is fixed within a fortnight, and she sends a photograph of herself using it.

choices.text: Promise someone will look, and stay on schedule.
choices.outcome: Someone does look, eventually. The ribbon is cut on time, by you, in a photograph that is very well lit.

title: The Parliamentary Question
body: Filed for oral answer. It is a good question, sharply drafted, and the honest answer is not flattering.

choices.text: Answer it straight.
choices.outcome: You concede the point and say what you are doing about it. The follow-up supplementary is gentler than it would have been, because there is nothing left to prise open. It is noted.

choices.text: Answer the question you wish had been asked.
choices.outcome: Technically responsive, substantively not. It is a skill and you are good at it and the clip is on the internet forever.

choices.text: Answer briefly, and promise the figures in writing.
choices.outcome: The written reply goes out in three weeks, when nobody is looking, which was the entire purpose.

0: Question Time. You answer the question that was asked, which is still noticed.
Seven questions this sitting. Your answers are short and true, and two of them make the news for being short and true.
1: Question Time. You answer a question that was nearly the one asked.
A sharp supplementary meets a smooth reply. Hansard records both; the papers record the reply.
2: Seven questions this sitting. The figures follow in writing, as promised, two weeks later.
You promise the figures in writing again. Your office has a template for the covering letter now.

variants.title: Question Time
variants.body: A Member has asked how many applicants to a well-announced scheme actually received anything. You have the number. It is eleven per cent.

choices.text: Give the number, and what you are doing about it.
choices.outcome: Eleven per cent, said aloud in the Chamber, followed by three changes. The supplementary is short, because there is nothing left to ask.

choices.text: Give the number of applications instead.
choices.outcome: Forty thousand applications, which is true and is not what was asked. The Member stands to say so, and the clip of her saying so does better than your answer.

choices.text: Say the figures will follow in writing.
choices.outcome: The written answer goes out on a Friday afternoon. It is read by the Member who asked, and by one journalist with a long memory.

variants.title: The Supplementary
variants.body: Your answer to the question went well. The Member rises for a supplementary, and it is the one your officials said would not come.

choices.text: Answer it straight, without the brief.
choices.outcome: You say you do not have the figure to hand, then say what you do know, which is enough. Your officials send a note that reads, in full, "Well handled."

choices.text: Answer a nearby question the brief does cover.
choices.outcome: The answer is fluent, confident and about something else. The Member says, "That was not my question," and is quoted the next morning in full.

choices.text: Offer to write to the Member with the details.
choices.outcome: You promise to write. The letter goes out three weeks later, when nobody is looking, and says what you could have said in the Chamber.

title: The Ministry Townhall
body: Four hundred officers. The anonymous question board has one item upvoted far beyond the rest, and it is about workload and it is not polite.

choices.text: Read it out and answer it.
choices.outcome: You read it in full, including the rude part, and then you answer it for eleven minutes without notes. The room changes temperature. It is the only thing from that townhall anybody repeats. It is noted.

choices.text: Address the theme without reading it.
choices.outcome: You speak warmly about wellbeing and the importance of sustainable pace. Four hundred officers understand precisely what has happened.

0: The townhall's top question is about workload again. You read it out, again. The upvotes have stopped being anonymous in spirit.
Four hundred officers, one microphone, and a rude question you read out in full. It is the only part anyone repeats.
1: The townhall's top question is about workload. You address the theme of it, warmly.
Your townhall slides circulate, unofficially, as an example of what a townhall can be.

variants.title: The Curated Questions
variants.body: This year's townhall questions were submitted in advance and curated. An officer at the back puts her hand up anyway.

choices.text: Take her question.
choices.outcome: It is about promotions, and it is fair. You answer it partly, and say that it is partly. Afterwards the curated questions are the part nobody remembers.

choices.text: Say there will be time at the end.
choices.outcome: There is no time at the end. There was never going to be, and four hundred officers watched her lower her hand.

variants.title: The Survey Results
variants.body: The ministry's engagement survey is back. Most numbers went up. One went down a long way: whether officers feel safe raising concerns.

choices.text: Put that number on the first slide.
choices.outcome: The first slide is the bad number, in large type, and you talk about it for ten minutes. Two directors look at the floor. Four hundred officers look at you.

choices.text: Lead with the numbers that went up.
choices.outcome: The deck opens on engagement, up four points. The other number is on slide nineteen. Most of the room found slide nineteen before you started.

title: A Year Without Incident
body: Everything runs. The schemes run. You go to Bintan in June and nothing breaks while you are gone, which is either a compliment or a warning.

choices.text: Use it to fix something nobody asked you to fix.
choices.outcome: You get a process fixed that has annoyed eleven thousand people for a decade. It takes a year and it is never announced.

choices.text: Use it to build your network.
choices.outcome: Coffee, lunches, and a very great deal of being remembered. It is not work. It is, unmistakably, the job.

choices.text: Use it to rest.
choices.outcome: You rest. It turns out you needed it more than the ministry needed the other two options.

0: Nothing breaks. You suspect this is not a coincidence, and cannot prove it.
You use a quiet year to fix a process that has annoyed people since before you arrived. It is never announced.
1: A quiet year, and forty lunches. You remember thirty of them, which is about average.
You attend everything you are invited to. By December, you are invited to more.
2: Bintan in June. You check your email twice, which is progress.
A quiet year. Somewhere, someone writes "steady" about you and means it kindly.

variants.body: No crisis, no reorganisation, no parliamentary question with your name in it. Your diary has white space for the first time in years, and everyone around you has noticed, and is pretending not to.

choices.text: Use it to fix something small and permanent.
choices.outcome: You fix the thing that has made every new joiner's first week worse for a decade. Nobody thanks you. The new joiners never find out what it used to be like.

choices.text: Use it for the lunches you keep postponing.
choices.outcome: Eleven lunches, four dinners and one kopi at a hawker centre that turns out to matter more than the dinners. People remember you now in a way they did not.

choices.text: Use it to sleep.
choices.outcome: You sleep. Your doctor, who has been saying things for three years, says nothing, which is the nicest thing a doctor has ever said to you.

variants.body: A year so uneventful that the most discussed thing around you is the new coffee machine. It has nine settings. Everyone uses the same one.

choices.text: Read every file you have been forwarded and never opened.
choices.outcome: You find two things that matter and one that should have mattered three years ago. You fix the two and write a note about the third that nobody will enjoy receiving.

choices.text: Make yourself useful to the people who decide things.
choices.outcome: You become the person who knows where things are. It is not a title, but it is the next best thing.

choices.text: Take your leave, all of it.
choices.outcome: You take all of it. The building does not fall down, which is either reassuring or the opposite.

title: The Counter
body: A redesign of the public-facing application process. The project team has never worked a counter. You worked one for four years.

choices.text: Tell them exactly why it will fail.
choices.outcome: You describe, from memory, the eleven things a person at that counter is actually holding in their hands. The room goes quiet. The design changes. Somebody senior asks where you worked before, and listens to the answer.

choices.text: Let them learn it from the pilot.
choices.outcome: The pilot fails in precisely the way you knew it would. You are asked to fix it, which is a smaller job than being listened to would have been.

title: The Last Paper
body: Six years of Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and one Saturday exam left. Half your cohort at work finished theirs at twenty-two, full-time, funded.

choices.text: Finish it.
choices.outcome: Second Upper. Nobody at work marks the occasion because nobody at work knew. It changes what you are eligible for, and it changes, more slowly, what you think you are eligible for.

choices.text: Defer. Work is at a critical point.
choices.outcome: The critical point passes and is replaced by another. You finish the degree four years later, by which time the eligibility it unlocks has moved.

title: Someone From Before
body: At an inter-agency meeting you recognise the chair. Years ago, before the degree, you sat two desks apart at the same statutory board, on the same grade.

choices.text: Speak to her afterwards.
choices.outcome: She remembers you immediately and without condescension, which you had not dared expect. She puts you on two committees that matter and tells you, plainly, which one to care about.

choices.text: Say nothing. She has moved on.
choices.outcome: She has not moved on; she simply did not see you. You think about the two desks for a week afterwards and then you stop.

title: The Board Takes a Second Look
body: A promotion board has been asked, unusually, to revisit an officer whose record does not match their grade. The officer is you.

choices.text: Make the case yourself, in writing.
choices.outcome: Four pages. You do not argue that you have been treated unfairly, which would have been true and useless; you argue what you would do with the next grade. The estimate is revised. Nobody tells you by how much.

choices.text: Let the record speak.
choices.outcome: The record does speak, and it is a good record, and it moves them slightly less than four pages would have.

title: The Figure, Cited
body: A review of the scheme's design cites a utilisation rate of 31%, attributed to a slide from your division. Someone senior asks, carefully, who presented it.

choices.text: Say it was you.
choices.outcome: He nods slowly. You watch your name move from one column of something to another.

choices.text: Say it was a team effort.
choices.outcome: It was not, entirely. Your team knows that, and it does you more good with them than the other answer would have done upstairs.

title: Paragraph Four
body: The consultancy's recommendations have been implemented, and have failed in exactly the way your minute paper, two years older, predicted in paragraph four. Someone has found paragraph four.

choices.text: Let paragraph four speak for itself.
choices.outcome: It is read aloud at a meeting you are not at. Afterwards, three people forward it to you, each believing they are the first.

choices.text: Offer to fix it.
choices.outcome: They let you. It takes a year, and a consultancy is engaged to evaluate your fix.

title: The Thing Nobody Announced
body: Every ministry that announced something at COS is now explaining delays. Your Minister, who announced nothing, is the only one who is not. He has noticed.

choices.text: Bring him the pilot, now that it is ready.
choices.outcome: He announces it at the next COS, on time and as described. He mentions your division by name, which Ministers do not do.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let him draw the conclusion.
choices.outcome: He draws it. When his Permanent Secretary next asks which divisions he rates, yours is the first he names, in front of the person who writes your ranking.

title: The Raw Feedback
body: A think tank has analysed the raw feedback you published. Its paper is cited in Parliament, approvingly, by both sides. Your Permanent Secretary forwards it to you with no comment, which from her is a great deal of comment.

choices.text: Reply with one line.
choices.outcome: "Thank you. It was their feedback." She replies within a minute, which nobody has ever seen her do.

choices.text: Write the follow-up nobody asked for.
choices.outcome: It becomes the template for the next national conversation, which uses four pillars.

title: The Decision Paper
body: The Inter-Ministry Committee has been dissolved. Its replacement has adopted your decision paper as its terms of reference, and someone has left your name in the footer.

choices.text: Leave your name on it.
choices.outcome: The footer travels further than you ever have. A Deputy Secretary you have never met asks for you by name.

choices.text: Take it off before it circulates.
choices.outcome: It circulates anonymously, which in this building is how people find out who wrote it.

title: The Third Point
body: The scheme has been amended, quietly, in exactly the way the third point suggested. A political reporter notices that you were the only office holder who said so in public.

choices.text: Take the question on the record.
choices.outcome: The piece runs on a Sunday. Its headline uses the word "candid", which your press secretary has asked you never to be again.

choices.text: Credit the post's author.
choices.outcome: He is astonished, then gracious, then a reliable critic for the rest of your career, which is a kind of compliment.

title: Hansard
body: A newer Member quotes you in her own speech, word for word, with attribution. Someone on the front bench looks up the original.

choices.text: Send her a note.
choices.outcome: She frames it. You hear about this from four people, none of whom are her.

choices.text: Say nothing.
choices.outcome: The quote goes round without you. It turns out to be the most-shared thing you have ever said.

title: Terms of Reference
body: A committee has been appointed to review political salaries. Your question in Cabinet appears, unattributed, as item three of its terms of reference.

choices.text: Make a submission under your own name.
choices.outcome: The committee thanks you for your submission. Its report adjusts the formula by a percentage point, which it describes as significant.

choices.text: Let item three do the work.
choices.outcome: It does very little work. But you were seen not to make a fuss, which is its own kind of item.

title: The Annual Report
body: The statutory board you were sent to fix has published its annual report. For the first time in four years it contains no restatements, and the auditors' letter is one page long.

choices.text: Ask to come back.
choices.outcome: You come back to a better office than the one you left. It turns out the secondment was a proving ground. Nobody tells you this; they simply act as if it had always been obvious.

choices.text: Ask to stay and finish it.
choices.outcome: You stay. The board becomes the case study on the leadership programme, taught by someone who was never there.

title: Polling Day, Again
body: Parliament is dissolved on a Tuesday. Nobody is surprised; the tents went up in the void decks a fortnight ago. This time your branch chairman has started using the word "swing" in sentences about you.

choices.text: Campaign on the record.
choices.outcome: You stand on a lorry and read out numbers. Some of them are your numbers.

choices.text: Walk every block, every night, for nine days.
choices.outcome: Nine nights, four hundred lift lobbies, one pair of shoes you will never wear again.

autoPlay.line: Polling day. You stand on a lorry and read out numbers, some of them yours.

title: The Indicators
body: Growth is strong and the forecasts are kind. Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets has to be settled now, and with it two of the four indicators the National Bonus is computed from. The indicators do not record who moved them.

choices.text: Push headline GDP.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Growth comes in a little under forecast, which in a strong year is noticed. The bonus is two months, which the newspapers describe as restraint.

choices.outcome: Growth comes in above forecast. Incomes at the 20th percentile rise too, slightly, in the way a small boat rises when a larger one goes past. The bonus is five months.

choices.text: Push incomes at the 20th percentile.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The 20th-percentile figure misses its target by a tenth of a point. No National Bonus is paid. The chart is still a good chart.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile grow faster than the median for the first time in six years. It makes a good chart, and a four-month bonus.

choices.text: Bank the targets. Change nothing that is working.
choices.outcome: The targets are met, exactly, as planned. The bonus is three months, which is what three months is for.

title: The Indicators, in a Downturn
body: The forecasts have turned. Exports are down for a third quarter and the word "retrenchment" is back in the papers. Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets has to be settled now, and the National Bonus will be computed from whatever it achieves.

choices.text: Protect jobs first.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: Unemployment rises anyway, by less than it would have. The indicator does not record the difference, and no bonus is paid.

choices.outcome: Unemployment holds. Growth does not. The bonus is two months, and a great many people keep jobs they will never know were on a list.

choices.text: Push growth through it.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The push does not take. Growth is flat, the 20th percentile falls, and no National Bonus is paid. Nobody calls it a gamble, because it was a plan.

choices.outcome: Growth recovers ahead of the region. The bonus is four months, and the speech about resilience writes itself.

choices.text: Cushion incomes at the 20th percentile.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The cushion holds the 20th percentile steady, which is not the same as growing it. No bonus is paid.

choices.outcome: The lowest incomes are protected through the downturn. The bonus is one month, which you mention to nobody.

title: The Indicators, Before an Election
body: A general election is due within the year. Your ministry's plan for the next three Budgets has to be settled before it, and everyone in the room is aware of the calendar, including, somehow, the indicators.

choices.text: Spread the gains widely before polling day.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The measures land after the indicators are measured. The bonus is one month. The measures are popular anyway, which was most of the point.

choices.outcome: The measures land in time and the indicators like them. The bonus is three months.

choices.text: Hold the line on the targets.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The targets are nearly met. The bonus is two months, and the campaign is a little quieter than your branch would like.

choices.outcome: The targets are met. The bonus is four months, and your branch asks, politely, whether anything at all could be announced.

choices.text: Push incomes at the 20th percentile.

nationalBonusRisk.outcome: The 20th-percentile figure misses by a tenth of a point, in an election year, which is the worst year to miss anything. No bonus is paid.

choices.outcome: Incomes at the 20th percentile rise faster than the median. The bonus is three months, and the chart is on a campaign flyer by Friday.

title: The Recruiter
body: A recruiter has found you on LinkedIn, which you did not know you were still on. A bank would like someone who understands how ministries think. The salary is a number you read twice.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your pass stops working on a Friday. On Monday you have a new one, and a view.

choices.text: Mention the offer, lightly, to HR.
choices.outcome: HR notes your "market value" and, for one ranking cycle, takes you more seriously. It is also noted.

choices.text: Decline. You are not finished here.
choices.outcome: You delete the message. Then you un-delete it, read the number again, and delete it.

title: The Consultancy
body: The firm that charged your ministry $1.9 million for a deck would like to hire someone who knows what ministries actually want. You are that person, apparently. The offer letter is on very good paper.

choices.text: Take it.
choices.outcome: Your first engagement is with your old ministry. The slides are beautiful. They say what your minute papers said.

choices.text: Decline, and tell them why.
choices.outcome: They take it well, and quote you in a thought-leadership piece about public-sector talent.

choices.text: Decline, and keep the letter in a drawer.
choices.outcome: The drawer is the top one. You open it more often than you would admit.

title: The Board Seat
body: A conglomerate would like a director who has been in Cabinet, or near it. The role involves four meetings a year and a fee the annual report lists in a footnote, which is the only modest thing about it.

choices.text: Resign your seat and take it.
choices.outcome: There is a by-election. It is described as a referendum on nothing in particular, and your successor wins it comfortably.

choices.text: Decline.
choices.outcome: You decline in writing, which you will later find was framed in the chairman's office as a curiosity.

title: The Board Seat
body: A conglomerate would like a director who has been in Cabinet, or near it. The role involves four meetings a year and a fee the annual report lists in a footnote, which is the only modest thing about it.

choices.text: Resign your seat and take it.
choices.outcome: Your GRC colleagues divide your ward between them. No by-election is required, which a constitutional lawyer explains to a newspaper at some length.

choices.text: Decline.
