choices.outcome: You decline in writing, which you will later find was framed in the chairman's office as a curiosity.

title: The Citizens' Panel
body: The ministry has convened a citizens' panel to review a scheme you once ran: twelve members of the public, chosen at random, three Saturdays. One of them is a retired schoolteacher from Ang Mo Kio who once wrote 340 words about it to the Forum page. He has brought the cutting.

choices.text: Tell him, privately, that you once looked up his address.
choices.outcome: He considers this for a long time. Then he says that in thirty years of teaching he looked up a great many addresses, and he hopes you were at least as worried as he usually was. The panel's report is fair. He wrote most of it.

choices.text: Thank him for his letter, in front of the panel.
choices.outcome: He accepts the thanks with the expression of a teacher accepting homework that has clearly been copied. The panel's report is fair, and has a section on responsiveness.

choices.text: Leave the sessions to your deputy.
choices.outcome: Your deputy reports that the panel was constructive, and that one member asked, twice, whether you would be attending.

title: The Promotion Board
body: A promotion board is considering your case. One of its four members is an officer whose posting you fought for in the reorganisation, years ago, before you placed yourself. She is a Director now. She has not declared an interest, because there is no field on the form for gratitude.

choices.text: Ask HR whether this needs declaring.
choices.outcome: HR consults its guidance, which covers family, finances and former employers but not gratitude, and to be safe replaces her with someone who has never heard of you. The board is very fair. You find this less comforting than you expected.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is not a conflict; it is a memory.
choices.outcome: She says very little in the board itself. She does not need to: she said it at lunch beforehand, to the chair, in one sentence about a reorganisation.

title: A Small Favour
body: Your friend at the agency, the one who told you about the flat three weeks early, has been in touch. His nephew has applied for a position in your ministry. He is, your friend says, very hardworking, and wants no special treatment, only for someone to look at it.

choices.text: Make sure someone looks at it.
choices.outcome: Someone looks at it. The nephew is interviewed, is in fact very hardworking, and gets the job on merit, probably. The flat and the nephew are now one story, and it is yours.

choices.text: Forward it to HR, declaring the connection.
choices.outcome: HR thanks you for the declaration and files it next to the application. The nephew is not shortlisted. Your friend says he understands, in the tone of a man updating a ledger.

choices.text: Tell him you can't, and why.
choices.outcome: You mention the flat. There is a pause on the line, and then he laughs and says that was public information, three weeks early. You agree that it was. Neither of you mentions the nephew again.

title: The Block Party
body: At a block party in your ward, a woman you do not recognise introduces you to forty of her neighbours. Years ago, on one of fifty-one Tuesday nights, a young volunteer at a Meet-the-People Session wrote an appeal for her that actually argued her case. It was you. She has told everyone, in detail, more than once.

choices.text: Let her tell it again.
choices.outcome: She tells it with improvements. By the end of the evening the appeal has overturned a decision, saved a business and possibly a marriage. Forty people will vote for the version with the marriage.

choices.text: Tell them the appeal worked because her case was good.
choices.outcome: This is true. She tells them you are being modest, and modesty is now part of the story, which is going round the block faster than you can walk it.

title: The Budget Committee
body: The officer who would have had the good box in the reorganisation, before you secured it for yourself, has had a perfectly good career anyway. She now chairs the committee that decides your division's budget. She is scrupulously fair to you, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Apologise, properly, over coffee.
choices.outcome: She lets you finish. Then she says she stopped thinking about it years ago, which you both know is the kind of thing people say. Your budget is approved in full. You will never know whether the coffee had anything to do with it.

choices.text: Make your bid on its merits and nothing else.
choices.outcome: It is a good bid. It receives exactly what a good bid receives from someone being scrupulously fair, which turns out to be four officers and half a system.

choices.text: Find out who else sits on the committee.
choices.outcome: Two of the other four remember the reorganisation too. One of them owes you. You spend a week arranging to be owed slightly more, and the bid passes.

title: Farewell Drinks
body: Your friend in HR, the one who once mentioned your CEP and then changed the subject, is leaving the service. At her farewell drinks, on her second glass, she tells you that a CEP is reviewed every year by people who mostly read your last two postings, and that the hard postings get read twice.

choices.text: Ask for the hardest posting going.
choices.outcome: You ask the next morning. HR says it will note your interest, and does, and eighteen months later you are sent somewhere difficult, and someone reads it twice.

choices.text: Thank her, and let her enjoy her drinks.
choices.outcome: You talk about her new job instead. She is going to a bank. She says the salary is a number she read twice.

title: The Interview Panel
body: The officer you quietly worked out was the source of the leak has done well since. She now sits on the interview panel for a post you want. She does not know that you know. You are almost sure of this.

choices.text: Say nothing. Compete on the record.
choices.outcome: She asks you two fair questions and one hard one. You answer all three. Whether she knows remains, as far as you can tell, entirely your problem.

choices.text: Let her understand, very quietly, that you know.
choices.outcome: You mention, in passing, a Telegram channel. She does not react at all, which is how you know. The post is yours. So, now, is something else.

title: Two Names
body: A journalist has noticed that the "Enhanced" scheme announced at Committee of Supply has the same budget line, the same eligibility criteria and the same hotline as the scheme it replaced. She would like to know which name people should use when they call.

choices.text: Say both names are correct.
choices.outcome: Both names are correct. She prints this. It reads exactly as well as it sounds.

choices.text: Say it is the same scheme, renamed, and explain what changed.
choices.outcome: What changed was the word "Enhanced". You say so. The piece runs with your quote in the headline and is, against all expectation, quite kind.

title: The Raw Data
body: A think tank has asked, with the usual courtesies, for the raw feedback from the national conversation you wrote up. The spreadsheet is still in a file. It is still eleven hundred people talking about the cost of living, and it still does not fit three pillars.

choices.text: Release it.
choices.outcome: The think tank's paper observes, politely, that the feedback and the report describe two different countries. Your Permanent Secretary asks why you released it. You say it was asked for. She says that is not usually the reason.

choices.text: Send the report again, with a covering note.
choices.outcome: The covering note is very good. The think tank thanks you for the report, which it already had, and files a second request, which is a different kind of note.

title: Officer A
body: Your recusal memo from the tender evaluation is now slide 14 of the procurement module every new officer takes. It does not name you. It calls you Officer A. At lunch, two of your juniors discuss Officer A, approvingly, in front of you.

choices.text: Tell them.
choices.outcome: They are delighted, and then slightly disappointed, the way people are when a parable turns out to be someone they report to.

choices.text: Say nothing, and finish your lunch.
choices.outcome: Officer A remains a better person than you, because Officer A never has to do anything else. You find you do not mind.

title: Lanterns
body: The grassroots adviser who mentioned, apparently in passing, that you handle yourself well with people would like to know if you are free on Saturday. It is a Mid-Autumn celebration at the community club. There will be lanterns, a lion dance and an MP, and the MP would like to meet you. This is also, apparently, in passing.

choices.text: Go, and stay to stack the chairs.
choices.outcome: You carry lanterns, are photographed with a lion, and stack chairs until ten. The MP notices the chairs.

choices.text: Send your apologies. You have a deadline.
choices.outcome: The deadline is met. The adviser says there will be other Saturdays, in the tone of someone who has written down which ones.

title: The First Cabinet
body: The colleague you backed in the succession is now Prime Minister. At his first Cabinet meeting he thanks everyone for their support, in general terms, and then looks at you for slightly longer than at anyone else.

choices.text: Ask for nothing.
choices.outcome: He gives you something anyway: the chair of a ministerial committee that meets on Saturday mornings. It is a mark of enormous trust, and you will never see a Saturday again.

choices.text: Ask for the hard portfolio nobody wants.
choices.outcome: He agrees before you finish the sentence, which tells you he had been hoping someone would ask.

title: The Other Life
body: Someone who went to tea in the year you declined is now a Minister. On the evening news she announces a scheme your people designed. She thanks the public service, in general terms, which is correct.

choices.text: Send her a note of congratulations.
choices.outcome: She replies by hand. She remembers the year you were both invited, and says she has wondered since which of you made the right choice. She does not say which way she has decided.

choices.text: Turn off the television and go back to the file.
choices.outcome: The file is better than the announcement. It usually is. That was, you remind yourself, more or less the reason.

title: The Younger Officer
body: A younger officer asks you, over kopi, whether she should go to tea. She has been invited. She does not know that you were too, once, or what was in your folder, or that the next email never came.

choices.text: Tell her to go, and to keep her folder thin.
choices.outcome: She goes. Two years later she is a candidate. She tells a newspaper that an older colleague once gave her the best advice she ever had, and does not say what it was, which is the advice working.

choices.text: Tell her about your folder.
choices.outcome: You tell her all of it. She listens the way you once listened at tea, thanks you, and you realise you have just been vetted by someone half your age.

title: A Model Ward
body: Your ward's swing has been written up in an internal party paper as a model. The organising secretary would like you to mentor three new candidates before the next election. They are young, earnest, and have each read the paper.

choices.text: Teach them the walkabout.
choices.outcome: You teach them how to listen to a stallholder about chillies on camera without looking like someone listening on camera. Two of them get it.

choices.text: Teach them Meet-the-People.
choices.outcome: You take them to a Tuesday night. One of them stays until midnight writing a letter that actually argues the case. You recognise the look.

title: The Improvement Plan
body: Your reporting officer has put you on a performance improvement plan. It has three objectives, a review in six months, and a line for your signature that is described, twice, as an acknowledgement rather than an agreement.

choices.text: Sign it, and do exactly what it says.
choices.outcome: You meet all three objectives, two of them early. The six-month review lasts eleven minutes and ends with the word "encouraging".

choices.text: Ask for a transfer before the review.
choices.outcome: HR finds you a post in a division with a new director, who reads files from the most recent page backwards. You start, in effect, again.

choices.text: Contest the assessment, in writing.
choices.outcome: Your reply runs to four pages and is filed with the plan. It changes nothing on paper and something in the room: your reporting officer now writes everything down.

variants.body: HR has scheduled a meeting called a "development conversation". It has an agenda, a template, and a second HR officer, who takes notes and does not speak.

choices.text: Agree to the objectives, and meet them.
choices.outcome: The objectives are measurable, which turns out to be a kindness. You meet them by October. The second HR officer is not at the review.

choices.text: Ask to be posted somewhere else.
choices.outcome: A post comes up in another division, with a director who prefers to form her own views. Your file arrives a month after you do.

choices.text: Put your side on the record.
choices.outcome: You write two pages, calmly. They are attached to the template, and the template is filed. The next conversation has no second officer in it.

variants.body: Your reporting officer would like to "set some clear expectations" for the next six months. There are six, numbered, and copied to a name you do not recognise.

choices.text: Meet every one of them, in writing.
choices.outcome: Six months, six expectations, six emails confirming each one met. The name you did not recognise replies to the last one: "Noted, thanks."

choices.text: Ask for a fresh start somewhere else.
choices.outcome: HR agrees briskly, as if it had been waiting for you to ask. The new division has never heard of you, which is the point.

choices.text: Reply to each expectation, point by point.
choices.outcome: Your reply is longer than the expectations. It is read carefully by the name you did not recognise, who now knows exactly who you are.

title: A Word from the Whip
body: The Party Whip would like a word, over kopi, about your attendance, your ward, and a speech the papers described as "brief". Nobody uses the word "plan". Everybody can see one.

choices.text: Promise to do better, and then do better.
choices.outcome: You speak in three debates and visit every block in your ward twice. The Whip's next note to you is one line long and says "Good."

choices.text: Ask to move to a committee where you can be useful.
choices.outcome: You are moved to a Government Parliamentary Committee that meets at eight in the morning. You are, it turns out, a morning person now.

choices.text: Explain, politely, that the ward comes first.
choices.outcome: The Whip agrees that the ward comes first, and notes that Parliament is also, technically, somewhere.

title: The Bed Crunch
body: Public hospitals are running at over ninety per cent bed occupancy, and emergency department waiting times are in the papers again. You have been asked for a paper on transitional care: beds outside the hospitals for patients who are well enough to leave and have nowhere ready to go.

choices.text: Recommend more transitional beds, and say where the nurses will come from.
choices.outcome: Your paper has a section on manpower that nobody asked for and everybody quotes. The beds are approved. The nurses are, as you said, the hard part.

choices.text: Recommend the beds, and leave the nurses to a later paper.
choices.outcome: The beds are approved quickly. A later paper, not yours, discovers the nurses. It cites yours as "an important first step".

choices.text: Recommend better discharge planning instead.
choices.outcome: It is the right answer and the less announceable one. The hospitals like it. The press office asks whether there is a version with a number in it.

title: The Premiums
body: MediShield Life premiums are due for review. The actuaries' number is the actuaries' number. The question in front of you is how to present it, over how many years, and with how much in subsidies alongside.

choices.text: Present the full number, with the subsidies next to it.
choices.outcome: The number is large and the subsidies are larger for the people who need them, and the slide says both. It is the least comfortable slide in the deck, and the only one nobody later has to correct.

choices.text: Phase it over three years, so no single year looks large.
choices.outcome: Each year looks reasonable. Somebody adds the three years together within a week, in a Forum letter with a table in it.

choices.text: Ask the actuaries to walk you through their assumptions first.
choices.outcome: Two days in a room with the actuaries. You come out understanding claims inflation better than anyone in your division, and slightly worried about it.

title: The Waiting Time
body: A resident's six-hour wait at an emergency department has been posted online, with photographs. The post has four thousand shares and one factual error. You will be asked about it at a community event on Sunday whether you prepare or not.

choices.text: Visit the emergency department on Saturday night, unannounced.
choices.outcome: You sit in the waiting area for two hours. Nobody recognises you, which tells you something about the waiting area and something else about you.

choices.text: Answer on Sunday with the figures, and correct the error.
choices.outcome: The figures are accurate and the error is corrected. The resident's reply is shared more widely than your answer.

choices.text: Say the wait was too long, and stop there.
choices.outcome: It was too long, and you say so in nine words. The clip is on the evening news. Your colleagues' faces suggest it was about eight words too many.

title: The Dormitory Standards
body: New standards for migrant worker dormitories: fewer beds to a room, more toilets, better ventilation, more space per worker. The operators have written to say the costs will be passed on. The employers have written to say they will not be absorbed.

choices.text: Hold the standards, and phase the deadline.
choices.outcome: The standards hold. The deadline moves twice, in writing, with reasons. Two years later the rooms are measurably less crowded, which is not a headline and is the point.

choices.text: Hold the standards and the deadline.
choices.outcome: Three operators complain to three different people about you, by name. The rooms are less crowded on schedule.

choices.text: Soften the space requirement for existing dormitories.
choices.outcome: Everyone is relieved, including you, briefly. The new dormitories meet the new standard. The old ones meet the old one, for longer than anyone said.

title: The Wage Ladder
body: Your division is extending the Progressive Wage Model to another sector. The union wants the ladder steeper. The employers want it longer. The workers in the sector, when you finally meet some, want to know when.

choices.text: Back the steeper ladder.
choices.outcome: The ladder is steeper than the employers wanted and shallower than the union asked for, which in tripartism is a win for everyone and a story for nobody.

choices.text: Broker the longer, gentler ladder.
choices.outcome: Everyone signs. The first rung is lower than you hoped. You tell yourself it is a ladder, and ladders are climbed.

choices.text: Take both versions back to the workers, and ask.
choices.outcome: They choose the steeper one and ask for it sooner. You write that down exactly, and it is in the paper that goes up, which is not where it usually goes.

title: The Retirement Age
body: The retirement and re-employment ages are going up again, in steps, by law. You are to explain it at a dialogue for older workers. The slides are excellent. The first question, from a cleaner in the second row, is not on any of them.

choices.text: Answer her question, not the slides.
choices.outcome: Her question was whether she could keep her job if her knees could not. You answer it properly, which takes the rest of the session. The slides go home unshown.

choices.text: Take the question offline, and follow up.
choices.outcome: Your office follows up within a week, with a contact at her employer and a scheme she had not heard of. She does not know who sent it. That is fine.

choices.text: Ask the union representative beside you to take it.
choices.outcome: He answers it well, with a detail about re-employment contracts you did not know. The photograph in the newsletter is of him, answering it.

title: The Classification
body: A new estate is being drawn up, and someone has to decide which projects are Standard, which are Plus and which are Prime. You have a map, a set of criteria, and three neighbouring blocks that are, in every way a resident would notice, the same.

choices.text: Apply the criteria exactly, and let the line fall where it falls.
choices.outcome: The line falls between two of the three blocks. Years later, two neighbours on the same corridor will have different rules for selling the same kind of flat, and both will know exactly why.

choices.text: Move the line so it follows the road.
choices.outcome: The road makes a tidy boundary. The criteria are footnoted. Nobody looks at footnotes, until somebody does.

choices.text: Write a note on the three blocks, and send it up.
choices.outcome: Your note asks a question nobody wanted asked. It is answered, eventually, in a way you can live with, by someone more senior who takes the credit for the question.

title: Ninety-Nine Years
body: A residents' committee from an estate built in the 1970s has written in. The letter is polite, well researched and asks one question: what happens to their flats when the lease runs out. The answer is in the policy. They have read the policy.

choices.text: Meet them, and explain it in person.
choices.outcome: Two hours in a void deck. You explain the policy, and then you listen to what it means to them, which is a different and longer conversation.

choices.text: Reply in writing, accurately and kindly.
choices.outcome: Your letter is accurate and kind. It is pinned on the noticeboard, beside the lift, where it is read by everyone and believed by most.

choices.text: Invite them to the consultation on redevelopment.
choices.outcome: They come, all eleven of them, with a folder. Their folder is better organised than yours.

title: The Million-Dollar Flat
body: A resale flat in a mature estate has sold for one and a half million dollars. It is a very good flat. The headline does not say that. Your phone has begun to buzz in the particular rhythm of a ministry with a question to answer.

choices.text: Point out, with numbers, how rare such sales are.
choices.outcome: The numbers are correct and reassuring. The comments under the article are neither.

choices.text: Say what the government is doing about supply.
choices.outcome: You list the launches. It is a solid answer and a forgettable one, which on this subject is a success.

choices.text: Say you understand why people are worried, and mean it.
choices.outcome: You do mean it, and it shows, and the clip travels. A colleague says, kindly, that understanding is not a policy. It is, you think, a start.

title: The Merger List
body: Cohorts are smaller every year, and a list of schools to be merged has to be drawn up. Every school on it has an alumni association, a school song, and a former principal who is still alive and writes letters.

choices.text: Draw the list on the numbers.
choices.outcome: The list is defensible line by line. The letters arrive line by line too, many of them beautifully written, and all of them signed.

choices.text: Keep the oldest names, whatever the numbers say.
choices.outcome: The old names survive. Two newer schools with stronger numbers do not, and their students will remember the year their school was described as "consolidated".

choices.text: Propose that merged schools keep both names.
choices.outcome: The names are hyphenated. The school songs are not, and the first combined assembly is, by every account, loud.

title: The Banding
body: Full Subject-Based Banding means students take subjects at different levels, which means timetables that no longer fit inside a class. A principal has written to say her teachers are now, in effect, air traffic controllers.

choices.text: Fund the timetabling software she asked for.
choices.outcome: The software works, mostly. Her teachers are now air traffic controllers with radar, which they say is an improvement.

choices.text: Send a guidebook and a hotline number.
choices.outcome: The guidebook is thorough and the hotline is staffed. Her reply thanks you for both in a tone you will remember.

choices.text: Spend a week in her school, and find out.
choices.outcome: You spend a week with a timetable on a wall the size of a car park. You come back with three changes that fit on one page, and they work.

title: The PSLE Question
body: A parents' dialogue. The topic is the joy of learning. The first question is about PSLE Achievement Levels, the second about tuition, and the third is from a twelve-year-old who has been brought along and wants to know why there is an exam at all.

choices.text: Answer the twelve-year-old first.
choices.outcome: Your answer is honest and does not entirely defend the exam. The child nods. Several parents write it down, which is either a good sign or the opposite.

choices.text: Take the questions in order.
choices.outcome: Achievement Levels, tuition, and then, briefly, the child, who has by now been taken outside for a drink.

choices.text: Explain how Achievement Levels work, carefully, with the chart.
choices.outcome: Everyone in the room understands the chart. Nobody in the room is reassured by it. You suspect the chart was never the problem.
